title: Detection of Botnet
summary: This strategy detects Botnet, the resource development technique in which an adversary acquires access to a network of compromised devices to use for proxying, denial of service, credential stuffing, or spam. It matters because the victim organisation is usually not the target: your hosts are the resource being rented, so the earliest sign is unusual outbound behaviour rather than an inbound intrusion. Detection relies on flow records for many short connections to many distinct destinations, DNS logs for algorithmically generated or high volume lookups, firewall logs for scanning and amplification traffic, and command and control beacon analysis from network security monitoring. It fails in practice because the same patterns appear in peer to peer software, content delivery traffic, and legitimate research scanning, and because botnet traffic is often low and slow across thousands of destinations.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for signs that your computers have been recruited into a botnet. A botnet is a group of infected machines controlled by one person. The detection watches for machines that suddenly talk to many unknown servers or send unusual traffic.
beginner.whyItMatters: An infected machine is used to attack other people, not just you. That can put your organisation on blocklists and damage your reputation. The traffic may also hide a more serious intrusion. Botnet traffic is often quiet and spread out, so simple rules miss it. Grouping connections by destination count is what makes it visible.
howItWorks: Network devices record each connection with its source, destination, and size.
The rule counts distinct destinations and failed connections per internal host.
A single host contacting many new addresses in a short time raises the score.
DNS logs add lookups with random looking names or very high request counts.
Beacon analysis flags regular connections of the same size at fixed intervals.
Hosts that match are checked against known peer to peer and update software before alerting.
beginner.example: Think of a telephone exchange in a small office. One employee making forty short calls to forty unknown numbers in an hour stands out, even if each call is harmless. Nobody knows what was said, but the pattern is wrong. The exchange record, not the call content, is what tells you to investigate that desk.
takeaways: Botnet infections make your organisation a participant, not only a victim.
Counting distinct destinations per host reveals activity that per connection rules miss.
Regular timing and identical connection sizes are strong signs of automated control traffic.

objectives: Explain what a botnet is and how it affects an organisation that is not the intended target
Identify flow, DNS, and firewall telemetry useful for detecting botnet participation
Measure distinct destination counts, beacon regularity, and connection size patterns
Separate peer to peer and update traffic from genuine command and control behaviour
Plan containment steps that isolate the host without breaking business software
dataSources: Network flow records with source, destination, port, byte counts, and connection duration
DNS resolver query logs with request volume and entropy of queried names per host
Firewall logs showing outbound connection attempts to many distinct addresses from one internal host
Network security monitoring alerts for beaconing patterns and known command and control ports
Proxy logs showing repeated uniform requests with identical user agent strings from a single host
logic: The pattern is one internal host behaving like a member of a group rather than like a user: a high count of distinct external destinations in a short window, repeated failed connections to hosts that never answer, queries for many random looking names, or connections of near identical size at regular intervals. The fields to correlate are the internal address, the distinct destination count, the interval regularity, the byte counts, and the query name pattern. Benign activity comes from peer to peer software, operating system telemetry, content delivery networks, and backup services, all of which use many destinations but with recognisable domains and stable timing. The malicious case shows an unapproved process, destination addresses with poor reputation, and a beacon interval that survives reboots.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Internal Host Contacting Many Unrated Destinations
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   category: firewall
# detection:
#   selection:
#     action: allowed
#     dst_reputation: 'unknown'
#   condition: selection | count(distinct dst_ip) by src_ip > 100
# level: medium
falsePositives: Peer to peer update clients and torrent software used legitimately in the business
Security scanning appliances and research crawlers that contact many external hosts by design
Content delivery and advertising traffic from browsers that generates many short connections
Software inventory and licensing agents that poll many vendor endpoints each day
tuningNotes: Baseline distinct destination counts per host class over a week, then set thresholds separately for servers, workstations, and security appliances. Allowlist known software update and peer to peer domains by registrable domain, and require a beacon regularity condition before raising severity. Scope the high severity rule to server networks where outbound browsing should not happen at all. Raising thresholds reduces noise but lets a low and slow botnet hide, so retain flow data and run a periodic report on hosts whose destination diversity grows gradually over months.
